```{r setup, include=FALSE}
suppressMessages({ library(dplyr); library(data.table); library(ggplot2); library(knitr) })
req <- here::here("requests", "2026-09-new-vs-established-nonprofits")
out <- file.path(req, "out")
fmt  <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
pct  <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), x)
young <- c("0-4", "5-9")
show_years <- c(1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2019, 2021, 2023)
```

## The ask

> Is the field shifting toward "new" nonprofits and away from established
> institutions? Is there any analysis of this, and can NCCS data surface
> whether it is real?

(Requester identity and the verbatim ask are in the gitignored `_private.md`.)

## Short answer

No, not in the IRS filing data. Organizations under ten years old account for
a **shrinking** share of nonprofit spending, and the decline is steady over
three decades. The share of *organizations* that are young has been roughly
flat, so the sector is not running out of new entrants; new entrants are
simply staying small, while spending concentrates in organizations founded
thirty or more years ago. Three independent ways of measuring organization
age agree. The literature review in `literature.md` found no published
evidence for a shift toward new organizations either, and several sources
pointing the other way.

What the IRS data cannot see: for-profit providers, and any organization too
small to file a Form 990 or 990-EZ (990-N postcard filers report no
financials). Both are discussed under limitations.

## Data and method

Three canonical NCCS artifacts, each pinned in `_pins.csv`:

- **CORE series, merged tier, 990 + 990-EZ, tax years 1989-2023**
  (`nccsdata::nccs_read_core`). One row per filing; deduplicated to one row
  per EIN and tax year (latest tax period). Filings with missing or
  non-positive total expenses are dropped. All subsections included; a
  501(c)(3)-only cut is reported as a sensitivity.
- **Geocoded unified BMF** (`nccsdata::nccs_read`), one row per EIN, for the
  IRS ruling date, subsection, and NTEE code.
- **E-file 990/990-EZ header and Part I summary tables, tax years
  2012-2023** (`nccs-efile` v2.1 catalog): the self-reported year of
  formation and current-year total expenses.

**Metric.** Total expenses, following the request. Expenses measure what an
organization disburses in a year, they are reported on both the 990 and the
990-EZ for the whole 1989-2023 span, and the size-concentration literature
(McKeever and Pettijohn 2014) is stated in expense terms. Shares are computed
within each tax year, so inflation does not affect them. Medians are
reported alongside shares because the young-cohort mean is driven by a
handful of fast scale-ups (Bradach and Kim 2016; Kelley et al. 2024).

**Organization age**, three ways, because each has a known flaw:

1. **IRS ruling year** (BMF). Available for every EIN back to the 1930s, but
   it lags founding by a year or more, and it is *reset* when an organization
   is reinstated after automatic revocation (a process that began in 2010).
   A reinstated 1965 charity looks like a 2013 startup. Filings whose ruling
   year postdates the tax year are the visible tip of this and are excluded
   from the age tables; their size is reported below.
2. **First appearance in the CORE panel.** Independent of the ruling date and
   immune to resets: an organization that filed a 990 in 1995 cannot be
   "new" in 2020. Left-censored at 1989, so the under-ten-years group is
   only complete from tax year 1999 onward; the chart starts it in 2000
   because 1999 is a thin year in the legacy files.
3. **Self-reported year of formation** on the e-filed return (Form 990
   header). The most direct measure of founding, but only for e-filed returns,
   which were incomplete before the tax year 2021 mandate.

Age groups are 0-4, 5-9, 10-19, 20-29, and 30+ years. "Young" means under
ten. Hospitals (NTEE E20-E24) and higher education (B40-B59) are shown
separately because they hold about 40% of all expenses in every year.

## Findings

### 1. Young organizations' share of spending has fallen by more than half since 1990

```{r core-share}
a <- fread(file.path(out, "core_by_age_ruling.csv"))
sh <- a[, .(exp = sum(exp_sum), n = sum(n)), by = .(tax_year, age_grp)][
  , `:=`(exp_share = 100 * exp / sum(exp), n_share = 100 * n / sum(n)), by = tax_year]
sh[, age_grp := factor(age_grp, levels = c("0-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20-29", "30+"))]
tab <- dcast(sh[tax_year %in% show_years], tax_year ~ age_grp, value.var = "exp_share")
kable(tab |> mutate(across(-tax_year, ~ pct(.x))), align = "lrrrrr",
      caption = "Share of total expenses (990 + 990-EZ filers) by years since IRS ruling")
```

```{r core-count}
tab <- dcast(sh[tax_year %in% show_years], tax_year ~ age_grp, value.var = "n_share")
kable(tab |> mutate(across(-tax_year, ~ pct(.x))), align = "lrrrrr",
      caption = "Share of filing organizations by years since IRS ruling")
```

```{r core-young-summary, include=FALSE}
ys <- sh[age_grp %in% young, .(exp_share = sum(exp_share), n_share = sum(n_share)), by = tax_year]
y90 <- ys[tax_year == 1990]; y23 <- ys[tax_year == 2023]
e30_90 <- sh[tax_year == 1990 & age_grp == "30+", exp_share]; e30_23 <- sh[tax_year == 2023 & age_grp == "30+", exp_share]
```

In tax year 1990, organizations under ten years old accounted for
`r pct(y90$exp_share)` of all expenses reported on Forms 990 and 990-EZ. By
tax year 2023 that share was `r pct(y23$exp_share)`. Over the same period
their share of *filers* moved only from `r pct(y90$n_share)` to
`r pct(y23$n_share)`. Organizations thirty or more years past their ruling
date went from `r pct(e30_90)` to `r pct(e30_23)` of expenses.

### 2. The pattern holds without hospitals and universities

```{r core-exhh}
x <- a[hosp_hied == FALSE, .(exp = sum(exp_sum), n = sum(n)), by = .(tax_year, age_grp)][
  , exp_share := 100 * exp / sum(exp), by = tax_year]
x[, age_grp := factor(age_grp, levels = c("0-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20-29", "30+"))]
tab <- dcast(x[tax_year %in% show_years], tax_year ~ age_grp, value.var = "exp_share")
kable(tab |> mutate(across(-tax_year, ~ pct(.x))), align = "lrrrrr",
      caption = "Share of total expenses excluding hospitals (NTEE E20-E24) and higher education (B40-B59)")
hh <- a[, .(share = 100 * sum(exp_sum[hosp_hied]) / sum(exp_sum)), by = tax_year]
```

Hospitals and higher education hold a near-constant
`r pct(min(hh[tax_year != 1999, share]))` to `r pct(max(hh$share))` of
expenses in every year except 1999 (`r pct(hh[tax_year == 1999, share])`;
tax year 1999 is a known thin year in the legacy CORE files, with about
196,000 filers against roughly 315,000 in adjacent years), so they are not
what drives the trend. Excluding them, the young
share falls from `r pct(x[tax_year == 1990 & age_grp %in% young, sum(exp_share)])`
in 1990 to `r pct(x[tax_year == 2023 & age_grp %in% young, sum(exp_share)])`
in 2023.

```{r fig-young-share, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.5}
c3 <- fread(file.path(out, "core_by_age_ruling_c3.csv"))[
  , .(exp = sum(exp_sum)), by = .(tax_year, age_grp)][, exp_share := 100 * exp / sum(exp), by = tax_year]
f <- fread(file.path(out, "core_by_age_firstseen.csv"))[
  , .(exp = sum(exp_sum)), by = .(tax_year, first_grp)][, exp_share := 100 * exp / sum(exp), by = tax_year]
ef <- fread(file.path(out, "efile_by_age_formation.csv"))[
  , .(exp = sum(exp_sum)), by = .(TAX_YEAR, age_grp)][, exp_share := 100 * exp / sum(exp), by = TAX_YEAR]
lines <- rbindlist(list(
  sh[age_grp %in% young, .(series = "Ruling year (BMF), all filers", share = sum(exp_share)), by = tax_year],
  x[age_grp %in% young, .(series = "Ruling year, excl. hospitals & higher ed", share = sum(exp_share)), by = tax_year],
  c3[age_grp %in% young, .(series = "Ruling year, 501(c)(3) only", share = sum(exp_share)), by = tax_year],
  f[first_grp %in% young & tax_year >= 2000, .(series = "First 990 in CORE panel (from 2000)", share = sum(exp_share)), by = tax_year],
  ef[age_grp %in% young, .(series = "Self-reported formation year (e-file)", share = sum(exp_share)), by = .(tax_year = TAX_YEAR)]
))
ggplot(lines, aes(tax_year, share, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(v) paste0(v, "%"), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Tax year", y = "Share of total expenses",
       title = "Organizations under 10 years old: share of nonprofit spending",
       subtitle = "Five definitions across three datasets; none shows a rising share", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 3))
```

### 3. Two independent age measures agree

**First appearance in the CORE panel** (no ruling date involved):

```{r firstseen}
f[, first_grp := factor(first_grp, levels = c("0-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20-29", "30+"))]
tab <- dcast(f[tax_year %in% c(2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2019, 2021, 2023)], tax_year ~ first_grp, value.var = "exp_share")
kable(tab |> mutate(across(-tax_year, ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), "", pct(.x)))), align = "lrrrrr",
      caption = "Share of total expenses by years since the organization's first 990/990-EZ in the CORE panel (panel starts 1989, so older groups are empty in early years)")
```

**Self-reported formation year** on e-filed returns:

```{r efile}
ef[, age_grp := factor(age_grp, levels = c("0-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20-29", "30+"))]
tab <- dcast(ef, TAX_YEAR ~ age_grp, value.var = "exp_share")
kable(tab |> mutate(across(-TAX_YEAR, ~ pct(.x))), align = "lrrrrr",
      caption = "Share of total expenses by years since self-reported formation, e-filed 990/990-EZ")
efc <- fread(file.path(out, "efile_coverage_by_year.csv"))
```

This is the shortest series but the most direct measure of founding, and it
is flat: organizations formed within the past ten years held about 5% of
e-filed expenses in every year from 2012 to 2023, with the under-five group
near 2%. Two coverage notes. The 990-EZ has no formation-year line, so this
measure covers full Form 990 filers only (the EZ filers, who are smaller and
younger, are the `r pct(100 * sum(efc$formation_missing) / sum(efc$filers), 0)`
of returns without a formation year; they hold
`r pct(100 * sum(efc$exp_formation_missing) / sum(efc$exp_total))` of expenses).
That is why the level here sits below the CORE ruling-year series. And
e-filing was optional before tax year 2021, so earlier years are a
self-selected sample; 2021-2023 are near-complete.

### 4. Where the young cohort's money sits: entrants, medians, and the top of the distribution

```{r entrants}
e <- fread(file.path(out, "core_entrants_by_year.csv"))
e[, `:=`(entrant_share_n = 100 * entrants / filers, entrant_share_exp = 100 * exp_entrants / exp_total)]
kable(e[tax_year %in% c(1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2019, 2023),
        .(tax_year, filers = fmt(filers), first_time_filers = fmt(entrants),
          `share of filers` = pct(entrant_share_n), `share of expenses` = pct(entrant_share_exp, 2))],
      align = "lrrrr", caption = "Organizations filing their first 990/990-EZ in the panel")
```

```{r medians}
med <- a[, .(exp_median = weighted.mean(exp_median, n)), by = .(tax_year, age_grp)]
med[, age_grp := factor(age_grp, levels = c("0-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20-29", "30+"))]
tab <- dcast(med[tax_year %in% c(2000, 2010, 2019, 2023)], tax_year ~ age_grp, value.var = "exp_median")
kable(tab |> mutate(across(-tax_year, ~ paste0("$", fmt(round(.x / 1000)), "k"))), align = "lrrrrr",
      caption = "Median total expenses by age group (nominal dollars; n-weighted across the hospital/higher-ed split)")
```

```{r top}
t <- fread(file.path(out, "core_top_filers_by_age.csv"))[, share := 100 * n / sum(n), by = .(tax_year, top)]
tab <- dcast(t[age_grp %in% young, .(share = sum(share)), by = .(tax_year, top)][tax_year %in% show_years],
             tax_year ~ top, value.var = "share")
kable(tab |> mutate(across(-tax_year, ~ pct(.x))), align = "lrr",
      caption = "Share of the 1,000 and 10,000 largest filers (by expenses) that are under ten years old")
```

Entry into the filing universe has slowed as a share of filers (about 8%
of filers were first-time filers in the late 1990s, about 4.5% in the
2020s), and first-time filers' share of expenses has fallen below half a
percent. Young organizations are also a shrinking share of the largest
filers. Together with the roughly flat count share, the picture is many
new organizations, each small, with the largest and fastest-growing budgets
sitting in long-established institutions.

### 5. Cross-check: how badly does the ruling date misstate age?

```{r xcheck}
xc <- fread(file.path(out, "xcheck_ruling_vs_formation.csv"))
xc[, share := 100 * n / sum(n)]
kable(xc[, .(`ruling year minus formation year` = gap_bucket, organizations = fmt(n), share = pct(share))],
      align = "lrr", caption = "E-filers with both a BMF ruling year and a self-reported formation year (one row per EIN, latest return)")
gap <- fread(file.path(out, "xcheck_gap_by_ruling_year.csv"))
```

```{r xcheck-fig, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(gap[ruling_year >= 1990 & ruling_year <= 2023], aes(ruling_year, 100 * share_gap_gt10)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1f78b4") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(v) paste0(v, "%")) +
  labs(x = "IRS ruling year", y = "Formed 10+ years before ruling",
       title = "A ruling date is not a founding date",
       subtitle = "Share of e-filers whose self-reported formation year is more than 10 years before their IRS ruling year") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r xcheck-nums, include=FALSE}
cv <- fread(file.path(out, "core_coverage_by_year.csv"))
cv[, `:=`(p_post = 100 * ruling_postdates / filers, p_exp_post = 100 * exp_ruling_postdates / exp_total)]
```

The ruling date misstates age for a meaningful minority: about one in eight
e-filers reports a formation year more than twenty years before its ruling
year, and among organizations with a 2023 ruling date roughly a quarter
were formed ten or more years earlier. Every such case biases the
ruling-year series *toward* finding young organizations, not against. Filings whose
ruling year postdates the tax year (the unambiguous cases) are excluded from
the ruling-year tables; they were `r pct(cv[tax_year == 1990, p_exp_post])`
of expenses in 1990 and `r pct(cv[tax_year == 2023, p_exp_post])` in 2023.
Because those excluded 1990 filings are overwhelmingly old organizations,
adding them back would lower the 1990 young share and make the decline
slightly smaller, not larger. The first-appearance and formation-year
measures, which do not have this flaw, show the same decline.

## Takeaways

- **The premise is not supported by IRS filing data.** Organizations under
  ten years old held about a fifth of nonprofit spending in 1990 and under a
  tenth in 2023. Their share of organizations barely moved. The sector keeps
  producing new organizations; it is not routing money to them.
- **Spending is concentrating in the oldest institutions**, and that is not
  only hospitals and universities, whose share is flat at about 40%.
- **Three age definitions across three datasets agree** on direction and
  roughly on magnitude, including the two that are immune to the
  ruling-date reset problem.
- **What this cannot rule out.** A shift toward for-profit providers (in,
  say, health care, child care, or education) is invisible in 990 data and
  would need BLS or Census ownership data. A shift of *attention* or *new
  grant dollars* toward young organizations that has not yet shown up in
  spending totals is also possible; the literature review found survey
  evidence pointing the other way (Candid 2025, 2026) but no direct measure.
  Government-grant and grants-paid fields in the e-file extraction could
  test the funder side next.

## Limitations

- 990-N filers (gross receipts normally under $50,000) report no financials
  and are absent from every table. Most post-2014 Form 1023-EZ entrants sit
  in that group (Candid 2025; Taxpayer Advocate 2018), so the young cohort's
  true spending is somewhat higher than shown, but by construction it is
  under $50,000 per organization.
- CORE tax years 1989-2011 are the legacy NCCS files; 2012 onward are IRS
  SOI extracts. The 2012 step in filer counts reflects that source change,
  and tax year 1999 is unusually thin (about 196,000 filers).
- Ruling year is missing for about 6% of BMF EINs (mostly pre-1970 records
  and sentinel values); those filings are excluded from ruling-year tables.
- Nominal dollars throughout; shares are unaffected, medians are not
  deflated.
